title: The prophets, again
tomorrow: one dad in a story Jesus tells does something odd. what?

lines: RULES ARE RULES. JUST THIS ONCE.
cards: A coach says rules are rules. A parent says just this once. A group chat splits down the middle over whether someone deserves a second chance.
Most weeks bring a fight like that. The prophet Micah imagines someone asking what to bring God. Calves?
Thousands of rams? Rivers of oil? Then the one-line answer, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God."

teach.b: Judgment, in that old English, means doing justice: treating people rightly, especially people with no one to stand up for them. Mercy is the kindness that doesn't let go. Micah won't pick one.

Hosea hears God say: "For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice." Jesus quotes that line back to critics who didn't like the company he kept at dinner. So here's what the prophets give for a week like this one.

teach.h: COLD WITHOUT MERCY, SOFT WITHOUT JUSTICE.
teach.b: Justice alone can turn cold: the rule is applied, the weak get flattened, and everyone calls it fair.
Mercy alone can turn soft: nobody is held to anything, and the strong keep stepping on the same people. The prophets hold both in one hand.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in Micah's line, the price of an offering doesn't climb.
He starts with calves, goes up to rivers of oil, even a firstborn child, and then turns the whole bidding war down. What God asks for there isn't bigger. It's three verbs: do, love, walk.

how: Catholics hear the prophets read at Mass, especially in Advent and Lent, and the Church's social teaching draws on them in its call to care for the poor and to work for justice.

o: messengers calling Israel back to God
priests who ran the Temple rites

games.q: the prophets' one hand — tap the pairs.
p: do judgment, love mercy, walk with God
I desired mercy, and not sacrifice
the old word for doing justice

s: a prophet in the Bible is mainly a fortune-teller
Micah and Hosea speak God's call to justice and mercy now, not just the future.
Jesus quotes Hosea's line about mercy and sacrifice
to critics who didn't like the company he kept at dinner.
Micah says God wants bigger offerings
he lists calves, rams and rivers of oil, then asks for justice, mercy and a humble walk.

games.q: your little brother broke a house rule and your parents are split: one wants a punishment, one wants to let it go. what would Micah's line suggest?
o: a fair consequence, given kindly, so he's both held and helped.
the toughest consequence, so everyone sees justice done.
no consequence at all, because mercy should always win.
games.why: Micah holds both in one line: to do judgment, and to love mercy. Neither one alone is what he asks.

practice: Choose one small unfairness near you this week: someone left out, shorted or not heard. Wish: picture what fair would look like. Obstacle: name what would stop you.
Plan: finish one sentence, if that happens, then I will, and hold the plan through the sit.

wordCard.voice: The prophets. Israel's messengers who called the people back to God, holding justice and mercy in one hand.

orig.note: Latin: mercy, the word in Micah 6:8 and Hosea 6:6 in the Vulgate.

carryVoice: Your line: justice and mercy. One without the other walks with a limp. See you tomorrow.
